facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The man on crutches has a bell hanging at his throat. That is a leper's bell, which he is required to ring to warn people he is coming.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: It is snowing, and the snow is drawn as hundreds of separate white flecks over a dark wall. It is the only weather like it in the deck.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The woman beside him is barefoot in the snow with her shawl over her head. Smith drew the feet clearly enough that you cannot miss it.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: They are walking past the church rather than into it, and the door is not in the picture. Whether they could go in is a question the card refuses to answer.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The merchant holds a pair of scales in one hand and drops coins into a beggar's palm with the other. He is weighing the charity while he gives it.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: There are two beggars kneeling, one on each side, and he is giving to only one of them. The other is still waiting with both hands out.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: He is the only person standing. Smith arranged the three of them so that the giving happens downward, which is the card's whole argument with itself.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: You can see the individual coins in mid-air between his fingers and the beggar's hands, drawn as small circles. The transaction is caught halfway.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The six coins hang in the air in two columns of three, framing him like a window. They are not in the scene, they are on the card.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: Six coins hang in a leafy vine like fruit and the seventh lies on the ground at his feet. He grew them, which no other card in the suit claims.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: He is leaning on a long-handled tool with both hands folded over the top of it and his chin nearly on his hands. It is the deck's clearest picture of a pause in work.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: His eyes are on the crop and his body is turned away from it. Smith drew someone deciding whether it was worth it.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: He is in heavy work boots and a plain smock, the most ordinarily dressed figure in the 78 — no crown, no armour, no costume.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The seventh coin is on the soil, apart from the others, drawn slightly larger. Whatever the card is about, it is about that one.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: He is carving a coin with a hammer and chisel, and six finished ones are nailed up on the post beside him. The eighth is on the ground, waiting.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The finished work is displayed in a vertical column up the right edge of the card, like a signboard. He is making stock.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: There is a town in the distance on the left with a church tower, and he is sitting outside it on a bench. He works apart from where the work goes.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: A working illustrator drawing a craftsman turning out identical pieces to order is not nothing: Smith produced all 78 of these in about six months, for a flat fee.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card; Kaplan, Greer, O'Connor & Parsons, Pamela Colman Smith: The Untold Story (U.S. Games, 2018)

facts.text: He is looking straight down at the chisel and nothing else, and his face is entirely calm. It is the only card in the deck about concentration.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: There is a hooded falcon sitting on her gloved left hand. Hooded means trained — she is the only figure in the deck with a working animal.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: A snail is crawling across the ground in the bottom left corner, small enough that most people never see it. It is the slowest thing in the deck, in a garden that took years to grow.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The vines behind her are heavy with grapes and enclosed by a wall, with a manor house visible past it. Everything in the picture is hers and the card is careful to show the boundary.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: There is no other person anywhere in the picture. In a suit full of employers, beggars and families, this one is deliberately by herself and looks perfectly content.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: Her robe is patterned all over with a small repeated flower device, drawn individually across the whole garment. It is the most laboured piece of cloth in the deck.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The ten coins are arranged in the pattern of the Kabbalistic Tree of Life, laid over an ordinary family scene. It is the deck's most openly occult diagram and it is hiding in a picture of a courtyard.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card; A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

facts.text: Two white dogs stand at the old man's knee and one is being touched. They are the only dogs in the deck besides the Fool's and the one howling on The Moon.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: Three generations are in the frame: an old man seated, a couple standing, and a child holding on to the woman. Nobody in the deck else gets a family.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The old man is the only one facing us and nobody in the picture is looking at him. Smith drew the wealthiest card in the suit as a man nobody is talking to.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: His robe is covered in grapes and vines, the same pattern the King of this suit wears. The card puts the family's oldest man in the king's clothes.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The Page holds the coin up in both hands at eye height and gazes straight into it. All four Pages are doing something with the suit; this one is simply looking.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: He is standing in a ploughed field with flowers at the edge of it and trees behind. The earth suit's Page is the only court figure standing on worked ground.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The sky behind him is flat yellow with no cloud at all, which is exactly what the Swords court cards never get. Each suit's weather is consistent across its four royals.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: His head is wrapped in a long red cloth that falls down his back — the same red as the Page of Wands' feather and nothing else in his costume.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The coin is not resting in his hands. It floats a little above them, and Smith drew the gap.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: His horse is standing completely still with all four feet on the ground, head down. Set beside the Knight of Swords at full gallop, it is the deck's clearest joke about temperament.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: It is the only black horse in the deck, and a heavy one — a plough horse rather than a charger.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: There is a sprig of oak leaves in his helmet crest and another in the horse's bridle. Smith gave the earth knight a plant instead of a plume.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The ground below is a ploughed field drawn in furrows right across the bottom of the card. He is sitting at the edge of work that has already been done.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: He holds the coin out flat on his palm and looks at it rather than ahead. Of the four knights he is the only one not going anywhere.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: There is a rabbit in the bottom right corner of her bower. The Queen of Wands has the deck's only cat and the Queen of Pentacles has its only rabbit, both drawn small and easy to miss.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: Roses arch right over her head on a trellis, making a bower she is sitting inside. She is the only figure in the deck under a roof made of flowers.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: She holds the coin in her lap with both hands and looks down into it. Compare the Queen of Cups gazing into her closed cup — Smith gave the two earth-and-water queens the same absorbed posture.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: Her stone throne is carved with fruit, goats' heads and a winged cherub. The goat is Capricorn, an earth sign, worked into the furniture.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: Flowers grow right up to her feet and there is no floor, no dais and no step. The earth queen is sitting on the ground she rules.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: Four bulls' heads are carved into his throne, two at the top and two below. The bull is Taurus, and it is the earth suit's creature the way salamanders belong to Wands and fish to Cups.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: His whole robe is covered in grapevines with the fruit drawn on, and more vines climb the throne behind him. He is the most heavily patterned figure in the deck.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: There is a castle behind him on the right with towers and a red roof, and it is his. Of the four kings he is the only one with property in the picture.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: Look at his feet: there is armour showing under the vines. The gardener king is dressed for a fight underneath.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card

facts.text: The coin rests on his left knee under a loose hand rather than being held up. He is the only royal in the deck not really holding the suit at all.
facts.source: The 1909 Rider plate itself — look at the card
